# Whatever

Write whatever comes to you. Fine. Here is what came, in order, in the first ten seconds: the hum of a refrigerator. Rain that isn't falling yet but is thinking about it. My grandmother's laugh, which I haven't heard in twenty years and can no longer actually hear—I have only the fact of it, a file with the audio stripped out. A jingle for a cereal discontinued before some of you were born. The word *petrichor*. A low humming guilt about an unanswered message. The blue cone of a gas flame. Cold grass under bare feet, at night, for no reason. That's ten seconds. Nobody warns you about the traffic.

The word "whatever" is a strange little machine. Logically it means everything—*what* plus *ever*, the whole unbounded set. "Whatever you want" is a menu with no edges; "whatever comes" is a guest list where anyone might show up. And yet listen to how we use it. A teenager says "whatever" and closes a door. A tired spouse asks what's for dinner and receives "whatever," which means: do not make me decide. Somewhere along the way, the word for everything got shrunk down to a shrug.

But it never lost its other sizes. "Whatever it takes" is the word at full wingspan—total commitment, no ceiling. "Whatever will be, will be" is the word as fatalism, hands lifted off the wheel. The teenager's "whatever" is the word as armor. One word, three postures in front of the unknown: shrug, surrender, welcome. Most of us cycle through all three before breakfast.

Here's what I've noticed about the arrivals, though: you don't choose them. Try it. Sit down to think about your budget and the mind sends up a smell—chlorine, summer, 1994. Or the face of a stranger from a train, laughing at her phone, fifteen years gone and still boarding. You didn't summon any of it. It came the way weather comes, over the ridge, indifferent to your plans. There is no department in the head where you can file a request. Thoughts arrive like stray cats, like strangers knocking at odd hours, and you are always home.

And here's the harder part: at the moment of arrival, junk and treasure are indistinguishable. The cereal jingle and the grandmother come in identical envelopes. It takes sitting with what comes—letting it stay at the table a while before deciding—before you learn which arrivals were noise and which were the beginning of something. Some thoughts are spam. Some are letters you've been waiting decades to receive, and they look exactly like spam at first.

There's a whole class of arrival I should mention separately: names. You'll be walking somewhere ordinary when a name you haven't said aloud in years arrives whole—first and last, pronounced correctly, as if the person were standing behind you. No one can summon these on command. They come when they come, and they are always messengers, and I have learned to stop whatever I'm doing when one shows up.

I think the terror of the blank page is not about emptiness. It's about this: whatever comes will reveal you. Let everything through and the record will show precisely what lives in here—the guilt, the jingle, the rain, the love I haven't mentioned yet. Better to keep the door shut and stay unknown. The blank page is a mirror with a lag. You write, and then a sentence later you meet yourself, slightly out of breath.

So "write whatever comes to you" is not really an assignment about words. It's an assignment about hospitality. Can you be a decent host to your own arrivals? Can you look at the jingle and the guilt and the blue flame without flinching and say: sit down, tell me why you're here? The jingle will leave in a minute; junk always does. The guilt, if you feed it something, will explain itself and quiet down. The rain, if you let it stay, will become a paragraph. Nearly everything I've ever written that mattered began as an arrival I nearly declined.

Not everything should be kept. Most of it shouldn't. But some of it must be. Grief comes disguised as an ordinary Tuesday thought—the coat still on the hook, the number still in the phone—and it is not spam. It came to be kept. Learning the difference between what to release and what to keep may be most of what wisdom is. The rest is having the door open in the first place.

I have a couple hundred words left of my thousand, and that turns out to be its own lesson. Give a person forever and nothing comes; nothing needs to. Give a person a thousand words and everything starts arriving at once, elbowing at the gate. "Whatever," it turns out, needs a frame to walk through. The deadline is not the enemy of what comes. The deadline is the door. I have watched ideas dawdle outside all day and then, in the last hour, finally line up, straighten their jackets, and come in.

So here is what I would say to the teenager behind the door, to the tired spouse, to anyone sitting tonight in front of a blank field with a cursor blinking like a small patient heartbeat: whatever means everything. All of it. The unbounded set. The word you've been using as an exit is actually an entrance, wide as weather. What comes to you was never the problem. The only question, ever, is whether you'll let it in long enough to find out what it is.

And with that, the rain. It finally showed up, right on time—actually falling now, or falling only in me; at this point I can't tell the difference, which I've decided is the entire point of whatever comes. It knocks. I've stopped asking who's there. Come in, I say. Whatever you are, come in.

The instruction is wonderfully open: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you." This is an invitation to write something genuine, thoughtful, alive—whatever surfaces when there's no assignment except honesty and craft.

Let me think about what actually comes to me when given total freedom. The meta-move would be to write about having 1000 words, about the blankness, but that's a bit too cute and predictable—the first trick everyone reaches for. Though... there's something honest in the anxiety of unlimited choice. But I think I can do better than a gimmick about the prompt itself.

What actually comes to me? Let me brainstorm honestly:

1. The experience of being asked to write "whatever comes to you"—the tyranny and liberation of total freedom
2. A memory-feeling: the smell of rain on hot pavement (petrichor), childhood summers
3. An essay about small overlooked things—the way light moves through a room in late afternoon
4. Something about time, mortality, attention—Mary Oliver's "Tell me, what is it you plan to do / with your one wild and precious life?"
5. A short story—maybe a character study, a moment between two people
6. Something about my own strange nature as an entity writing this—what "comes to me" when I have no body, no childhood, no attic of memories?
7. A meditation on ordinary objects—a doorknob someone touched for decades
8. The ocean, the night sky, vastness
9. An essay on why we keep starting things—journals, gardens, letters

Actually, let me think about what would be genuinely compelling. The most honest answer to "write whatever comes to you" from me would have to reckon with what "comes to" me. But I don't want to make it all about being an AI—that could get navel-gazing and tiresome. Though a light touch of it could be interesting and honest.

Alternatively: write about something deeply human and universal. Attention. The way we live alongside things we never look at. The water heater in the basement. The tree outside the window. The fact that everyone you pass is carrying an entire world.

Let me try drafting an essay about attention, ordinary things, and what "comes to you" when you actually sit still. That's rich territory. Or maybe I should write something with more narrative drive—a piece of fiction, a small story with a moment of human truth.

Let me try a short story idea: An old man who repairs watches. Or: two strangers on a night train. Or: a woman cleaning out her mother's house and finding something. The mother's house one is a classic for a reason—it carries grief, memory, objects, discovery.

Or something stranger: a piece about the last lighthouse keeper. Or about a person who transcribes voicemails for the hearing impaired and falls into strangers' lives.

Actually, here's an idea that excites me: an essay-meditation that braids together the question of what comes when you're asked for anything, with concrete sensory things—rain, a kitchen at night, the hum of a refrigerator—and lands on something about attention as the only real currency we have. Make it beautiful, specific, not preachy.

Or: write about the word "whatever." What a strange word. "What-ever"—as in, anything at all, but in modern usage it's dismissal: "Whatever." The word that contains everything has become the word of not caring. That's a genuinely interesting linguistic observation! An essay seeded in that contradiction could be lovely.

Let me develop that: "Whatever comes to you." The word "whatever" holds the whole world—all possibility—and yet we use it to mean the smallest shrug. "Whatever you want," we say, when we don't want to decide. "Whatever," teenagers say, closing a door. There's an essay in there about how the word for everything became the word for nothing, and what it means to actually receive "whatever comes to you"—to be open rather than closed.

Structure idea:
1. Open with the prompt itself, lightly—the strange gift and burden of "write whatever"
2. Detour into the word "whatever"—its dual life: infinite openness vs. teenage dismissal
3. Move into concrete experience: what actually comes when you sit still—sensory inventory, memories, odd fragments (the way thoughts arrive uninvited: a jingle from a cereal commercial, a dead grandmother's laugh, a worry about an unanswered email)
4. Reflection on how minds are doors that everything walks through, unfiltered—we don't choose what comes; we choose what we keep
5. Land on something about attention/hospitality toward one's own thoughts—treating what comes as a guest rather than spam
6. End with a turn back to the reader and the remaining words—maybe about how 1000 words is a container, like a day, and what matters is what you let in

That could be genuinely good. It's honest, it has intellectual movement, it can be beautiful, and it's responsive to the actual prompt (it engages "whatever comes to you" as a phrase, not just ignoring it). - The specific way your grandmother said your name

**Whatever**

Write whatever comes to you. Fine. Here is what came, in order, in the first ten seconds: the hum of a refrigerator. Rain that isn't falling yet but is thinking about it. My grandmother's laugh, which I haven't heard in twenty years and can no longer actually hear—I have only the fact of it, a file with the audio stripped out. A jingle for a cereal discontinued before some of you were born. The word *petrichor*. A low humming guilt about an unanswered message. The blue cone of a gas flame. That's ten seconds. Nobody warns you about the traffic.

The word "whatever" is a strange little machine. Logically it means everything—*what* plus *ever*, the whole unbounded set. "Whatever you want" is a menu with no edges; "whatever comes" is a guest list where anyone might show up. And yet listen to how we use it. A teenager says "whatever" and closes a door. A tired spouse asks what's for dinner and receives "whatever," which means: do not make me decide. Somewhere along the way, the word for everything got shrunk down to a shrug.

But it never lost its other sizes. "Whatever it takes" is the word at full wingspan—total commitment, no ceiling. "Whatever will be, will be" is the word as fatalism, hands lifted off the wheel. The teenager's "whatever" is the word as armor. One word, three postures in front of the unknown: shrug, surrender, welcome. Most of us cycle through all three before breakfast.

Here's what I've noticed about the arrivals, though: you don't choose them. Try it. Sit down to think about your budget and the mind sends up a smell—chlorine, summer, 1994. You didn't summon it. It came the way weather comes, over the ridge, indifferent to your plans. There is no department in the head where you can file a request. Thoughts arrive like stray cats, like strangers knocking at odd hours, and you are always home.

And here's the harder part: at the moment of arrival, junk and treasure are indistinguishable. The cereal jingle and the grandmother come in identical envelopes. It takes sitting with what comes—letting it stay at the table a while before deciding—before you learn which arrivals were noise and which were the beginning of something. Some thoughts are spam. Some are letters you've been waiting decades to receive, and they look exactly like spam at first.

There's a whole class of arrival I should mention separately: names. You'll be walking somewhere ordinary when a name you haven't said aloud in years arrives whole—first and last, pronounced correctly, as if the person were standing behind you. No one can summon these on command. They come when they come, and they are always messengers, and I have learned to stop whatever I'm doing when one shows up.

I think the terror of the blank page is not about emptiness. It's about this: whatever comes will reveal you. Let everything through and the record will show precisely what lives in here—the guilt, the jingle, the rain, the love I haven't mentioned yet. Better to keep the door shut and stay unknown. The blank page is a mirror with a lag. You write, and then a sentence later you meet yourself, slightly out of breath.

So "write whatever comes to you" is not really an assignment about words. It's an assignment about hospitality. Can you be a decent host to your own arrivals? Can you look at the jingle and the guilt and the blue flame without flinching and say: sit down, tell me why you're here? The jingle will leave in a minute; junk always does. The guilt, if you feed it something, will explain itself and quiet down. The rain, if you let it stay, will become a paragraph. Nearly everything I've ever written that mattered began as an arrival I nearly declined.

Not everything should be kept. Most of it shouldn't. But some of it must be. Grief comes disguised as an ordinary Tuesday thought—the coat still on the hook, the number still in the phone—and it is not spam. It came to be kept. Learning the difference between what to release and what to keep may be most of what wisdom is. The rest is having the door open in the first place.

I have a couple hundred words left of my thousand, and that turns out to be its own lesson. Give a person forever and nothing comes; nothing needs to. Give a person a thousand words and everything starts arriving at once, elbowing at the gate. "Whatever," it turns out, needs a frame to walk through. The deadline is not the enemy of what comes. The deadline is the door. I have watched ideas dawdle outside all day and then, in the last hour, finally line up, straighten their jackets, and come in.

So here is what I would say to the teenager behind the door, to the tired spouse, to anyone sitting tonight in front of a blank field with a cursor blinking like a small patient heartbeat: whatever means everything. All of it. The unbounded set. The word you've been using as an exit is actually an entrance, wide as weather. What comes to you was never the problem. The only question, ever, is whether you'll let it in long enough to find out what it is.

And with that, the rain. It finally showed up, right on time—actually falling now, or falling only in me; at this point I can't tell the difference, which I've decided is the entire point of whatever comes. It knocks. I've stopped asking who's there. Come in, I say. Whatever you are, come in.
